title: NumPy: Broadcasting & Tensor Slicing
subtitle: 3D Cube Grid (3, 4, 3) · Stride Slicing & Shape Math
summary: Click slice operations (arr[0, :, :], arr[:, 1:3, :], or arr + vector) to pull active sub-cubes out of a (3, 4, 3) 3D tensor with live shape math.
intuition: Think of a 3D NumPy tensor of shape (3, 4, 3) as a stack of 3 transparent ice-cube trays, where each tray has 4 rows and 3 columns. Slicing arr[0, :, :] pulls out the entire front tray; slicing arr[:, 1:3, :] pulls out the middle two rows across all three trays; and broadcasting arr + vector clones a 1D row vector across every tray and row without copying a single byte of RAM!

howItWorks.title: Allocate Contiguous 1D Buffer
howItWorks.detail: NumPy stores all 3 × 4 × 3 = 36 numbers in one flat C-array and tracks shape=(3,4,3) and byte strides.

howItWorks.title: Select Slice or Broadcast Operation
howItWorks.detail: Choose arr[0, :, :], arr[:, 1:3, :], or arr + vector to inspect which indices are selected.

howItWorks.title: Compute Stride Offsets (Zero-Copy View)
howItWorks.detail: Basic slicing adjusts the start pointer and strides in O(1) time without duplicating data.

howItWorks.title: Align Trailing Axes for Broadcasting
howItWorks.detail: When adding a (3,) vector to (3, 4, 3), NumPy virtually expands it to (1, 1, 3) → (3, 4, 3).

howItWorks.title: Execute Vectorized SIMD Math
howItWorks.detail: CPU AVX/NEON instructions process contiguous chunks 50x–100x faster than Python for-loops.

evaluationChart.title: Execution Latency: Python Loop vs. NumPy (100k Ops)
evaluationChart.description: Contiguous C-backed ndarray memory eliminates Python interpreter loop overhead.

advantages: 50x–100x faster than nested Python lists via SIMD C loops.
Zero-copy views for slicing (arr[0, :, :]) and virtual broadcasting.
Universal array interface shared by Pandas, Scikit-Learn, and PyTorch.
limitations: CPU-only (use PyTorch/CuPy for CUDA GPU execution).
Homogeneous dtype per array (unlike mixed-type Pandas DataFrames).
Accidental broadcasting of (N, 1) + (1, N) can silently allocate O(N²) RAM.
applications: Image/video batch tensor manipulation (B, H, W, C)
Vectorized linear algebra & neural layer math

formulas.description: Integer indexing drops an axis; range slicing preserves the axis with reduced length.

formulas.label: Right-Aligned Broadcasting
formulas.description: Dimensions of size 1 stretch virtually across the matching axis.

codeTemplates.fromScratch:
import numpy as np

arr = np.arange(36).reshape(3, 4, 3)
print('Full shape:', arr.shape)

# 1. Pull out front tray
slice_0 = arr[0, :, :]        # shape (4, 3)
# 2. Pull out middle two rows across all trays
slice_mid = arr[:, 1:3, :]    # shape (3, 2, 3)
# 3. Broadcast (3,) vector across last axis
vec = np.array([10, 20, 30])
broadcasted = arr + vec       # shape (3, 4, 3)
print('Broadcasted shape:', broadcasted.shape)
codeTemplates.production:
import torch

arr = torch.arange(36).reshape(3, 4, 3)
slice_0 = arr[0, :, :]
slice_mid = arr[:, 1:3, :]
vec = torch.tensor([10, 20, 30])
broadcasted = arr + vec
print('PyTorch shapes:', slice_0.shape, slice_mid.shape, broadcasted.shape)
codeTemplates.dataPrep:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({'f1': [1, 2, 3], 'f2': [4, 5, 6], 'f3': [7, 8, 9]})
# Convert Pandas DataFrame to contiguous NumPy tensor
arr_2d = df.to_numpy(dtype=np.float32)
arr_3d = arr_2d.reshape(1, 3, 3)
print('Ready tensor shape:', arr_3d.shape)
